title: Woman had sex with dolphin in CIA operation to unlock alien contact

WARNING: GRAPHIC CONTENT Margaret Howe Lovatt recalled trying to teach a dolphin the English language at a NASA-funded lab - but she ended up having sex with him

07:00, 02 Oct 2026

One woman thought she was helping NASA communicate with aliens but found herself in a sexual relationship with a dolphin named Peter.

‌

‌

Margaret Howe Lovatt had a lifelong interest in animals and how they communicated with each other, leading her to play a crucial role in a 1980s experiment with one of the most sophisticated animal communicators - dolphins.

‌

In 1963 Margaret was living on the Caribbean island of St Thomas when her brother-in-law mentioned a secret lab at one end of the island where they were researching dolphins.

‌

Margaret, then only 20, drove out there for a look - and was welcomed by Gregory Bateson. He was the director of the lab and was immediately taken with the young woman who had asked if she could do anything to get involved.

Margaret had no training and was just a keen animal lover but she also had a talent for identifying animal communication patterns.

Grgeory permitted Margaret to observe the dolphins and document everything she noticed - despite lacking scientific training, she had a knack for identifying animal behaviour, securing her place in the study.

Margaret remembers meeting three of the dolphins. She said they were: "Peter, Pamela and Sissy. Sissy was the biggest. Pushy, loud, she sort of ran the show.

"Pamela was very shy and fearful. And Peter was a young guy. He was sexually coming of age and a bit naughty."

‌

The unusual project was set up to determine whether or not the dolphins could be trained to understand, and speak, English.

Along with Margaret's help, an ordinary home was transformed into a dolphin co-living space by flooding the downstairs with water.

‌

This meant those working on the project could live with the animals and observe them 24 hours a day. And as Margaret spent more times with the creatures, she formed ever closer bonds with them - especially Peter.

She explained: "Peter liked to be... with me. He would rub himself on my knee, my foot or my hand and I allowed that.

"I wasn't uncomfortable - as long as it wasn't too rough. In the beginning I would put him on the elevator and say you go play with the girls for a day.

‌

"It was just easier to incorporate that and let it happen, it was very precious and very gentle, Peter was right there, he knew that I was right there."

Margaret claims this became a regular part of her studies, as she tried to teach Peter to speak English.

‌

She said: "It was sexual on his part - it was not sexual on mine, sensuous perhaps. It would just become part of what was going on like an itch, just get rid of that we'll scratch and we would be done and move on. I was there to get to know Peter, that was part of Peter."

However, when the experiment's funding dried up, the pair were separated and Peter was transported 1,000 miles away to a small lab in Florida.

But the separation proved too much for the seemingly heartbroken Peter, who died just a few weeks later in what appeared to be an act of suicide.

‌

"I got that phone call from John Lilly. John called me himself to tell me. He said Peter had committed suicide," Margaret told The Guardian.

The lab's vet, Andy Williamson, attributed the dolphin's death to a broken heart, saying: "Margaret could rationalise it, but when she left, could Peter? Here's the love of his life gone."

‌

Ric O'Barry, from animal rights organisation The Dolphin Project, also supported the description of Peter's death as "suicide", adding: "Dolphins are not automatic air-breathers like we are. Every breath is a conscious effort. If life becomes too unbearable, the dolphins just take a breath and they sink to the bottom. They don't take the next breath."

The lab had been established by American neuroscientist, Dr John Lilly, who had been studying large-brained marine mammals for years.

He aspired that his experiment on the Caribbean island would allow the dolphins to produce human-like sounds through their blow holes, facilitating communication with humans.

Dr Lilly obtained NASA's financial support as he believed it would enhance the understanding of other intelligent life forms who utilise a different form of communication.

However, what began as an innocent experiment soon became mired in controversy by the time it was shut down.

Not only was there Margaret's relationship with Peter, but there were also whispers that the dolphins had been mistreated when they were given LSD.
